items.title: Fee-Only Financial Planning With No Minimums
items.summary:
Many consumers assume professional financial planning is available only after they've accumulated a large investment portfolio. That assumption is understandable. 

Traditional wealth management firms often require $500,000, $1 million or more in investable assets before accepting a client. Brokerage and insurance firms may be easier to find, but their representatives may be paid to sell investments, annuities or insurance products.

Yet millions of people need financial advice long before they become wealthy. 

A young couple may be deciding what kind of home they can afford An employee may need help evaluating retirement plan choices or stock compensation Parents may be weighing college funding against retirement savings A widow may need guidance after the death of a spouse A retiree may want a second opinion before claiming Social Security These consumers may not need ongoing investment management. They may need several hours of objective advice, a limited-scope project or a comprehensive financial plan. 

The Garrett Planning Network was built around the idea that they should be able to obtain that help without first meeting a large asset minimum, purchasing a financial product or transferring their portfolio to an advisor.

items.title: Is Your Homeowners Insurance Stuck in 1995?
items.summary:
Quick, which part of the U.S. gets natural disasters?

If you answered that hurricanes belong to Florida, wildfires to California and tornadoes to Kansas, congratulations, you have a perfectly good map of the situation before 1995. Now, fold it up and put it in the glove box next to the Thomas Guide.

That map is out of date. Like, ridiculously out of date, and our changing climate is loading the dice for bigger fires, heavier rain and longer heat waves, and it is doing it in places where you used to hear, "That doesn't happen here." Yes, that includes where you live. 

Check out some of the clips I've put on X and you'll see.

But don't take my word for it. Let's look at what has actually happened, followed by what you can do about it.

What we've been through recently In January 2025, wildfires tore through Los Angeles , killing at least 29 people and destroying or damaging more than 14,000 structures. I know this one personally because hundreds of my office's clients lost their homes. 

Scientists at World Weather Attribution found that a warming climate made the hot, dry, windy conditions behind those fires about 35% more likely. It was more like a tsunami fire than a wildfire.

items.title: Ask the Editor: Questions on Investments and Year-End Tax Planning
items.summary:
Each week in our Ask the Tax Editor series, Joy Taylor, The Kiplinger Tax Letter editor, answers questions on topics submitted by readers. This week, she's looking at four tax questions from readers on year-end tax planning strategies involving taxable investment accounts. ( Get a free issue of The Kiplinger Tax Letter or subscribe .) 

1. Tax-loss harvesting Question: I have lots of capital gains in my taxable investment account this year. My financial advisor suggested I sell some stocks that have gone down in value to minimize the tax hit. Is this a good tax move? 

Joy Taylor: Tax-loss harvesting (or capital-loss harvesting) is a popular way for investors to lower their federal income tax bills. The strategy involves selling stocks or other securities in your taxable investment accounts that have declined in value for the purpose of generating capital losses to offset capital gains from the sales of winners that you have sold during the year. Investors commonly do this closer to the end of the year, when they have a better idea of the amount of capital gains they will have.

If you are planning to sell stock you own at a loss to offset capital gains and then buy the same stock back soon thereafter, watch out for the wash-sale rule . You can’t deduct a capital loss from a sale of securities if you buy substantially identical securities up to 30 days before or after the sale. The recognized loss isn’t gone forever; it’s only suspended. That’s because the loss is added to the tax basis of your replacement securities.

items.summary:

The first, Your Diversified ETF Isn't as Diversified as You Think , examined how popular ETFs concentrate exposure to the AI capital spending cycle; the second, AI Is a Supply Chain Rather Than an Industry: Here's Why , mapped the supply chain layers behind that spending; the third, How to Manage the 4 Risks Hiding Inside Every AI-Heavy Portfolio , examined the risks facing the buildout itself. 

A new frontier AI model now reaches the market every few weeks. No hospital system, manufacturer, bank or retailer refreshes its production technology stack on that schedule, and none ever will.

That mismatch is not a minor operational footnote. It is a structural risk sitting underneath the valuation of nearly every company in the AI supply chain, because those valuations assume enterprise revenue will arrive on the same clock as model releases. It won't.

Two clocks running at different speeds Model providers compete on speed. The frontier model release cadence compressed dramatically through 2025 and into 2026: Labs that once shipped a major model roughly every six months moved to a pace of multiple substantive releases per week by early 2026, with one industry tracker counting more than a dozen meaningful frontier launches in the first quarter alone.

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

items.title: How Volunteering Builds Workplace Empathy
items.summary:
In more than 35 years managing people and culture, most recently as chief operating officer at Affinity Federal Credit Union, I've learned that the qualities that make someone good at serving members rarely start in an office. 

Empathy, patience and the instinct to listen before reacting usually are intangibles that develop somewhere else first, and then they show up at work.

A credit union runs on members trusting that the person helping them actually understands their situation. That kind of understanding is hard to teach in a training room. It's much easier to build in the middle of a real situation, with a real person, where there's no script to fall back on.

What a workshop can't recreate There's a difference between describing empathy in a session and actually experiencing it. A training module can explain active listening. It can't put someone in front of a stranger whose life looks nothing like their own and force them to figure out, in real time, what that person actually needs. But hands-on community service does exactly that.

I've watched employees come back from a volunteer project and engage differently almost immediately. They ask more questions before jumping to a solution, notice hesitation or frustration faster, and listen more than they used to.

items.title: Retired and Ready to Game? Why You Should Join the Grand Theft Auto 6 Craze
items.summary:
Pursuing your passion in retirement means different things to everybody. For some, it's perfecting their golf swing; for others, it's tending to a garden or traveling the globe. For a growing number of older adults, it’s booting up a gaming console and playing what is shaping up to be the biggest game launch ever — Grand Theft Auto 6. 

The first new installment of this widely popular game in over a decade was just released and has already set a record with $1.65 billion in pre-order revenue from over 17 million copies sold. 

While Boomers and Gen Xers may not be the immediate audience you think of, the first GTA came out in 1997. That means nostalgia may bring them back to the controller.

We're in a whole new world this time 

(Image credit: Getty Images) This iteration of the game drops you into the Miami-inspired Vice City, set within the state of Leonida. There, players are tasked with navigating a sprawling underworld of heists, street races and turf wars as Lucia and Jason. 

A lot has changed in the 13 years since GTA 5, which means players get a much improved experience. The graphics are dramatically sharper and more lifelike, and the gameplay feels more dynamic. For instance, how the story unfolds shifts based on the choices you make, and your character physically evolves based on your habits. 

If you hit the gym, you’ll bulk up; skip it, and you won't. Even the non-playable characters around town react differently to you depending on your reputation, appearance and behavior, making the world feel real. 

Older adults are gaming too

items.title: 4 Ways Generational Wealth Goes Beyond Money
items.summary:
What is generational wealth ? We often think about it in terms of money: A person or family has generational wealth when they have enough to pass on from one generation to the next — and this is true. 

But a family's legacy includes more than money. It also includes the assets that help the next generation build a truly wealthy life.

With that, here are four assets — beyond money — that parents can pass on to their children, and practical ways to get started.

1. Health Parents can pass on health by modeling healthy habits while sharing family health history. The next generation benefits from seeing how to manage diet and stress, and from knowing which hereditary risks to be aware of.

The everyday angle: Share healthy habits, visibly and vocally. Invite your kids to cook a healthy meal with you, and feel free to process out loud: "I'm feeling stressed, so I'm going for a long walk after dinner." Share your family health history with your adult children, including major conditions on either side of the family and at what age they appeared.

The financial angle: You might walk your young adult through your health insurance policy, explaining premiums, deductibles and out-of-pocket costs. Share how you balance coverage and costs, so they can also make informed choices.

Remember that short-term capital gains (assets held for one year or less) are taxed at ordinary income tax rates, different from those for long-term capital gains.

items.title: Which Types of ETFs Belong in a Taxable Brokerage Account?
items.summary:
An ordinary taxable brokerage account may lack the tax advantages of a Roth IRA or a 401(k) , but it beats both handily when it comes to flexibility. There are no annual contribution limits, income restrictions on eligibility or age-based withdrawal rules.

So you can deposit and withdraw your money whenever you choose, making accounts with brokers and trading platforms useful for financial goals that don't necessarily revolve around retirement. But this flexibility means you must account for taxes.

Investment returns in a brokerage account can receive different tax treatment depending on their source. Indeed, you may encounter short- and long-term capital gains , non-qualified and qualified dividends , ordinary interest income and return of capital.

These aren't all taxed at the same rate, and depending on the investment and where you live, they can create liabilities at both the federal and state levels. Providers of exchange-traded funds ( ETFs ) are well aware of this, which helps explain the increasingly diverse roster of funds designed to defer or minimize specific forms of tax drag.

Some accomplish this through the securities they hold, while others employ specialized management techniques and derivatives such as options . The trade-off is that these active ETFs can be more complicated and expensive than their plain-vanilla counterparts.

Tax efficiency also depends on your circumstances and your financial goals , meaning the fund with the lowest apparent tax burden isn't necessarily the best choice for all investors.

items.t: Which Types of ETFs Belong in a Taxable Brokerage Account?

items.title: Should You Convert Part of Your 401(k) Into a Lifetime Annuity?

As more Americans fear outliving their money and seek guaranteed income streams beyond Social Security, a growing number of workplace plan providers are adding ways to convert a 401(k) balance into a guaranteed lifetime paycheck. 

Offering in-plan options to turn a nest egg into a monthly paycheck, while still in its early stages, is a retirement savings innovation that is gaining momentum. Demand for retirement income solutions is climbing. Nearly all (91%) of plan participants responding to a J.P. Morgan Asset Management survey expressed interest in "in-plan guaranteed retirement income solutions.” And about four in five workers find purchasing annuities over time in a target-date fund appealing, according to the 2026 EBRI/Greenwald Retirement Confidence Survey . 

"Lifetime income is one piece of that larger retirement income picture that every individual is looking to put together," says Matt Tufano , senior client portfolio manager at Vanguard. "The role of a lifetime income solution is to provide more income stability and address longevity and the risk of outliving assets. It's another tool in the toolkit."

items.title: $63 Million Family Dollar Settlement: How to Get Your Refund Check
items.summary:
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) along with 17 states filed a complaint on November 12 alleging that Family Dollar, a nationwide discount retailer, has been overcharging its customers for years. According to the complaint, "Family Dollar routinely charges more at checkout than the prices displayed on its shelves, in its weekly circulars, and on its website and mobile app."

Family Dollar agreed to settle the complaint for $63 million – including $40 million in refunds to eligible customers – and to implement a pricing accuracy program that will be independently reviewed and certified annually. 

For customers who have relied on the discount retailer for low prices on everyday essentials, the news is a sigh of relief as Family Dollar will soon be taking steps to make sure prices are accurate. But it's also a reminder to scrutinize your receipts and be a more skeptical consumer in general. 

What does the FTC complaint against Family Dollar say? The November complaint filed by the FTC cites repeated customer complaints about cashiers and store managers refusing to honor the prices shown on store shelves or in advertisements. This allegedly resulted in millions of dollars in overcharges as customers paid more at checkout than they expected based on advertised prices.

The issue, according to the FTC, stemmed primarily from the retailer's practice of automatically updating prices at the point of sale (the cash register) without ensuring that shelf labels or online list prices had been updated as well. 

But the FTC also cites complaints that Family Dollar frequently refused…

items.title: 5 Steps to Take When an Inheritance Causes Anxiety
items.summary:
For many adult children, an inheritance leads to difficult questions about how to spend that money and what would make their parents proud. 

That can cause feelings of anxiety and stress, especially when the inheritance comes as a surprise. 

What heirs often underestimate is how emotionally challenging it can be to make even small, straightforward decisions with that money.

When emotions run high, choosing how to use your inheritance to "do the right thing" can add to the pressure many adult children already feel. But with the right approach, you can create a plan to confidently manage an inheritance — even if you weren't left with instructions on what that might mean. 

Moving past difficult feelings Many adult children who inherit money struggle with grief, guilt and frustration. These emotions can make an inheritance feel like a burden and add to the stress of figuring out how to move forward responsibly. 

Sometimes parents leave their children what's known as a letter of wishes . While it's not a formal legal document, it can provide helpful guidance on how to spend an inheritance without feeling as much guilt and anxiety.

items.title: IRS Increases Tax Credits for Families and Workers: What Changes for 2027
items.summary:
Claiming family tax credits is a must if you're eligible. Not only can family tax breaks lower your tax liability , but they might increase your refund. 

But which credits you qualify for can change from year to year. The amounts of the credits can also change, since many are adjusted yearly for inflation. 

For instance, the child tax credit has increased by $100 compared to last year, and that's not counting other family tax breaks. Here's what you can expect for the 2027 tax year (for income tax returns normally filed in early 2028). Read on.

Child Tax Credit 2027 The federal child tax credit is worth $2,300 per qualifying child for 2027 taxes. 

However, the maximum refundable portion is worth $1,800. That’s more than you could claim for 2026 tax returns. Plus, there's another caveat: To claim the CTC, both the child and the taxpayer (parent or guardian) must have Social Security numbers. For more information about the current child tax credit, see Who Qualifies For The Child Tax Credit? 

Note: Don't forget about state child tax credits . Currently, 17 states and the District of Columbia offer their own version of the child tax credit. Check your state's Department of Revenue website to see whether one is available to you. 

IRS Adoption tax credit in 2027 The federal adoption tax credit for the 2027 tax year (taxes generally filed in 2028) is worth up to $18,250 (up from $17,670 last year).

The adoption credit might be used for qualified adoption expenses paid to adopt a child and as an exclusion from income for employer-provided adoption assistance. But you can't…

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.
